description: We are a group of STEM October students
summary: Fireium is a web-based platform that articulates NASA's combustion research in ways including data charts, SI chatbots, PDF reports, and prediction models, in addition to mapping research gaps. Fireium allows researchers and engineers to predict the behavior of fire in different habitats (space station, moon base, etc.) by matching it to a specific NASA experiment after ranking them based on match accuracy. In the case of untested conditions (conditions that don’t match any of the NASA investigations), the platform maps them as a research gap. Beyond that, the platform is equipped with an SI chatbot, providing personalized resource navigation while maintaining factual consistency, as every claim is cited to its source (the sources consist only of the 3530 passages from NASA documents). Furthermore, the platform provides 4 different levels of data navigation ranging from beginner to expert, serving a broad audience with variable expertise.
details:
1. What our project does

FIreium is a web platform that collects, analyzes and organizes NASA’s combustion data in order to give useful fire-safety insights, and improve the understanding of fire behavior under different conditions (space stations, spacecraft, pressurized rovers, and bases on the Moon and Mars)

NASA has studied fire without gravity for decades. The results are spread across many sources:

  • 24 combustion investigations in the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository
  • 2,005 rows of measured test data in 22 run tables
  • 3530 scientific passages
  • fact sheets, NASA videos, history pages and Spinoff articles

The project aims to provide insights to the behavior of fire in microgravity in variable levels of expertise, encompassing undergraduate students, graduate students, aerospace engineers and researchers.

Our platform does exactly that. It does three things, and every feature is built around them:

  1. Starts from the habitat. Choosing a crew environment re-orders the whole site around that atmosphere: the ranking, predictions, research gaps and Mission Report.
  2. Never invents. Every statement on the site, including every AI answer, leads back to a NASA source with its page number. Code checks this; the model is not trusted to do it alone.
  3. Says how sure it is. Predictions carry a confidence score. Missing data is shown as a research gap instead of being hidden or guessed.

 

2. How it works, feature by feature

2.1 Start page:

What it does

  • Four guided paths follow, each marked with its level. Based on the expertise of the user, the website creates customized highly detailed plan for the user to offer optimal learning efficiency:

 

2.2 Research Explorer: all 24 NASA investigations

What it does

  • First, the user chooses a habitat then the page generates a short summary which includes 3 main parts: the safety requirements for the environment, the main findings from NASA’S research about the environment, and the research gaps which are the weakly researched aspects of the environment.
  • Along with the environment summary the page lists all the investigations in the selected environment. These experiments can be filtered by fuel state, material, safety area (prevention, detection, suppression), gravity, facility, topic, and the oxygen, pressure and airflow ranges tested. ==

How it is built

  • Data pipeline:
    • fetch_psi.py downloads every PSI combustion record, run table and image.
    • build_db.py normalises them into a SQLite database (flame.db): investigations, tables, runs, text passages.
  • Search: the text search matches word stems, so "smoke detection" also finds records that say "detector".
  • Range filters: a range filter keeps an experiment only if its tested range overlaps the requested one. An experiment that never reported a value is never matched as if it had.

Investigation profiles. Each investigation has its own page with:

  • a plain-language summary written by our team, clearly labelled as ours
  • NASA's own record text, copied unchanged
  • test conditions, run data, publications and related experiments
  • links to the NASA PSI record and the dataset DOI
  • what the official NASA resources say about that experiment

2.3 AI Research Assistant

Our AI Assistant uses only relevant NASA documents as a primary source of information and cites these documents in the generated answers so that the user can verify the accuracy of the claims and to prevent made-up answers. An example of the citation feature would be like:

    • 7 of 8 statements cite NASA.
    • 2 of 2 numbers were found in the cited passage.
    • 4 passages are cited, with page numbers.
    • 0 citations had to be removed.

If no relevant NASA data is found to answer the question, the assistant assigns a “research gap” tag to the answer so that the user knows that there is little or no research on the topic. Additionally, to increase accessibility, the AI assistant can adjust the wording level from student to expert, and the user can limit the searchable experiments to only a few experiments.

How it is built (research.py, retrieval.py)

  1. Library. NASA reports, science documents and analysed-data sheets are read page by page with pypdf (build_docs.py). The 10 official challenge resources are read too: web pages, PDFs and the video captions (build_resources.py). Together with the PSI records this gives 3,530 searchable passages, each tagged with its kind (NASA report, PSI record, run table, NASA resource and so on).
    • keyword search (TF-IDF, scikit-learn) catches exact names such as "PMMA" or "BASS-II"
    • meaning search (the BAAI bge-small-en-v1.5 model, run on our own server with FastEmbed and ONNX, with no paid API) catches passages that answer the question in other words

The two rankings are merged with reciprocal rank fusion.

  1. Ask. The best passages go to Claude (Haiku, low effort) as numbered sources. The instructions say: answer only from these sources and cite them.
    • every citation must point to a passage the model was actually given, or it is removed
    • the answer is split into statements, each labelled with the kind of evidence behind it
    • every number with a unit is looked up in the cited passage
    • sentences where the model talks about its own sources instead of NASA's findings are removed
  2. Stream. The answer streams in and is written out word by word, without the page jumping.

Without an AI key the same search runs and the passages are quoted directly, so the site still works and nothing is generated.

2.4 Fire Safety Insights: prevention, detection, suppression

What it does

This page explains the three main themes of the challenge using NASA's own evidence. Prevention covers material flammability, oxygen limits and airflow. Detection covers smoke and particle sensing. Suppression covers CO₂, helium and other gases that put flames out. The page uses NASA photos, small charts and word-for-word quotes, and it ends with a 10-question quiz so the user can test what they learned.

How it is built

Every point on the page carries a quote from a PSI record, the challenge text or an official NASA resource. When the server starts, verify() looks for each quote in its source. If one cannot be found, the server refuses to start, so the page can never drift away from the data.

2.5 Lessons & Applications: history, physics and Earth

What it does

This page is divided into four sections and includes a second quiz:

  1. Lessons from accidents: Apollo 1 (1967), Apollo 13 (1970) and the Mir fire (1997), taken from NASA's own history pages.
  2. Earth vs. microgravity: explains why a candle flame becomes a sphere in microgravity, and shows the Saffire-II table of the same materials burned in orbit and on Earth.
  3. Next-generation equipment: what NASA's records point to for future detectors, suppression systems and material tests.
  4. Uses on Earth: three NASA Spinoff technologies (firefighters' air tanks, fire detectors and fire-resistant clothing), plus ground testing in drop towers.

Drop towers are used to test fire on Earth. A falling package is weightless for a few seconds, which is enough time to light a flame and watch it. The page links two facilities:

  • NASA Glenn: 5.18 s of free fall, a combustion rig, and a centrifuge for partial gravity.
  • ZARM Bremen: 4.7 s of free fall, or 9.3 s with the catapult. Its GraviTower can reproduce Moon and Mars gravity.

This points directly at the biggest gap we found, which is that none of the 24 investigations were run in partial gravity.

2.6 Charts: NASA's measured data, interactive

What it does

The Charts page lets the user explore NASA's measured data directly:

  • Build your own chart from 18 NASA run tables. The chart can be a scatter, line, bar, histogram or box plot, coloured by any column.
  • Upload your own CSV file and chart it the same way.
  • Choose from 8 ready-made charts that show key results.
  • Download the plotted data as a CSV file, or open the original NASA file.

The "Where has NASA tested?" chart plots 1,009 NASA tests by oxygen and pressure against the cabin atmospheres of the five habitats. The Moon Base box shows at a glance which tests are relevant to it, and that no solid-material test falls inside it.

How it is built

  • Charts are drawn in the browser with Plotly, using run-table rows served by the API.
  • Each ready-made chart names real column names, and verify() checks them at startup, so a chart can never show a measurement that NASA's table does not contain.
  • Notes warn the user where a column means something different, for example oxygen measured in the burner gas rather than in the chamber.

2.7 Experiment Ranking: which NASA results matter for your habitat

What it does

Every investigation gets a relevance score from 0 to 100 for the chosen habitat. For Moon Base, FLEX ranks first (77.4), followed by ACME BRE (72.6) and FLEX-2 (70.5). Each card also says where its points came from, for example "oxygen match (+25), fire-safety directness (+18.8)".

How it is built (environments.py)

  • Seven factors are scored from 0 to 1 using the database: fire-safety directness, gravity relevance, oxygen match, pressure match, cabin-material relevance, ventilation data, and whether run data is available.
  • The habitat atmospheres are taken from the NASA challenge text. For example, the Moon is described as "30% or greater, with a corresponding pressure of 10.2 psi or less".
  • The user can drag the weight sliders or choose a safety focus (prevention, detection or suppression), and the ranking updates live.
  • The AI can also rank the experiments by a criterion that the user writes in their own words, and it cites the reasons.
  • The page states clearly that this is the project's own method and not a NASA score, and it shows the formula and the breakdown of every result.

2.8 Compare: two to four experiments side by side

What it does

The page starts with three summary boxes: what the selected experiments have in common, where they differ, and what information is missing. A full table follows, row by row. Suggested pairs (BASS-II vs BASS, SAME vs SAME-R, FLEX vs FLEX-2) make it quick to get started, and the AI can interpret the comparison on request.

How it is built

The rows come straight from the database. A missing value is shown as "Not reported" and is never filled in by guessing.

2.9 Predictions: what would a fire do in this atmosphere?

What it does

The Predictions page answers three questions: how fast a fuel droplet burns, whether the flame will go out, and how hot a gas flame gets. The user can either choose a habitat or set the oxygen, CO₂, helium and pressure levels manually. The page then gives a prediction with a likely range, a confidence score, and how the result changes compared with normal cabin air. In the example above, methanol burns at about 0.66 mm²/s at Moon Base air, with 87% confidence. The user can also upload a CSV file of conditions, and every row will be predicted.

How it is built (models.py, predict.py, scikit-learn)

The models follow strict rules so that the predictions can be trusted:

  • Tested on unseen data: the tests use 5-fold cross-validation grouped by test day, so tests run on the same day are never split between training and testing.
  • Must beat a guess: a model is offered only if it cuts the error of the no-model guess by at least 20%. Two candidate models failed this test (CFI-G ignition and burn time), so they are not shown, and the code says why.
  • Confidence falls with distance: the score drops and the likely range widens as the request moves away from real NASA tests. Outside a tested range the result is labelled as an extrapolation.
  • Impossible inputs are refused: an atmosphere whose gases add up to more than 100% gets no number.
  • Labelled as a prediction: every output says "model prediction, not a NASA measurement".

2.10 Research Gaps: what NASA has not tested

What it does

The gap map crosses what was burned with the oxygen level tested, or with other pairs that the user picks. It shows how many investigations fill each cell, and red dashed circles mark the empty combinations. With all 24 investigations there are 11 empty combinations. For example, no solid material has been tested above 22.5% oxygen, yet a Moon base will have 30% or more. The page also lists the main gaps and suggests research questions.

How it is built (gaps.py)

Everything is counted from the database for the investigations that pass the user's filters. A gap means "not in this NASA collection", and never a claim that no such research exists anywhere. The page says this clearly.

2.11 Mission Report: one click, one PDF

What it does

For any habitat, the page builds a fire-safety report with a reference list. The report is previewed on the page and can be downloaded as a PDF. It has six sections:

  1. The environment
  2. An AI-written briefing from NASA sources
  3. The most relevant experiments
  4. Fire-safety insights
  5. Research gaps
  6. The model estimate

The report can also be focused on prevention, detection or suppression.

How it is built (mission.py, fpdf2)

The report does not compute anything new. Each part comes from the module that owns it (ranking, insights, gaps and predictions), so the report always agrees with the rest of the site. Every statement carries a reference.

2.12 NASA Resources: full transparency on the data

What it does

This page lists the 10 official NASA resources for the challenge. All 10 are used, which adds up to 19 documents, 231 passages and 36,644 words, and every quote is checked. For each resource, the page shows:

  • what share of its text was read and used
  • which parts of the site use it (AI assistant, data pages, experiment pages, Insights, Lessons and Research Gaps)

Any file that could not be read is listed together with the reason, instead of being hidden.

3. Benefits

  • For mission planners and engineers: a ranked and cited answer to "which NASA results apply to my habitat?" in minutes instead of weeks of reading, plus a PDF report that is ready to share.
  • For researchers: fast search across 3,530 NASA passages with page-level citations, side-by-side comparison, interactive charts of the raw run data, and a map of untested conditions to guide new experiments.
  • For students and teachers: four levels of explanation, two quizzes, NASA photos and real data to learn from and teach with.
  • For everyone: trust, because every number can be traced to NASA and every prediction says how sure it is.

4. Intended impact

Fire is one of the most dangerous emergencies in space. There is nowhere to escape, and help is days or months away. As NASA prepares for long stays on the Moon and missions to Mars, crews will live in oxygen-rich, low-pressure atmospheres where fire has barely been studied.

Our goal is to make sure that this knowledge is used:

  • Show what is already known: bring NASA's decades of combustion results to the people designing future habitats, in a form that they can act on.
  • Show what is still unknown: gaps such as partial gravity and solid materials above 22.5% oxygen become a clear agenda for the next experiments, including affordable ground tests in drop towers.
  • Teach the next generation: students learn fire safety in space from real NASA data, at their own level.

5. Tools, languages and software

 

 

Data

  • NASA PSI combustion repository: 24 investigations, 22 run tables, PSI images and documents.
    • NASA Combustion Science
    • the Researcher's Guide to ISS Combustion Science
    • the NASA ScienceCast video and its captions
    • Apollo 1 and Apollo 13 (NASA Safety Center)
    • the Mir fire (NASA History)
    • three NASA Spinoff articles, read in full from NASA's Technical Reports Server
  • NASA Glenn's drop-tower facility page and ZARM Bremen, for ground testing.

6. How the project is creative

  • Habitat first, not database first: instead of another list of experiments, the site asks where the crew will live, and re-orders all of NASA's evidence around that atmosphere.
  • An AI that is checked by code: most AI tools only ask the model to be accurate. Ours removes citations that point to nothing, looks up every number in its source, and shows the reader a ledger of how well each answer is backed.
  • Predictions that admit their limits: models are offered only if they beat a simple guess on unseen test days. Confidence falls away from real tests, and models that failed the test are openly left out.
  • Missing data becomes a result: the Research Gaps map and the habitat chart show where NASA has not tested, and link to the facilities that could close those gaps.
  • One source of truth: the Mission Report, the AI and every page draw on the same checked data, so they can never disagree.

7. Factors our team considered

  • Accuracy over impressiveness:
    • Every quote is verified at startup.
    • Every model prediction is labelled as a prediction, never as a NASA measurement.
    • Our own methods (the relevance score and the plain-language summaries) are labelled as ours, not NASA's.
  • Honest limits: each model lists what it does not cover, for example droplets are not cabin fabrics. A research gap means "not in this collection", not "never studied".
    • We chose a small, fast model (Claude Haiku, low effort), which costs about $0.002 and takes 4–11 seconds per answer.
    • Meaning search runs on our own server at no cost per question.
    • The whole site fits on a small cloud server with 512 MB of memory.
  • Accessibility and design: light and dark modes, phone and desktop layouts, motion that respects "reduce motion" settings, and keyboard shortcuts.

  • Testing: a 100-check test suite runs locally. An end-to-end test of the live site checks every page and feature, including real AI answers and PDF downloads.
